#+title: Agent skills
#+description: The skill as a construct in agent tooling: the SKILL.md format, its frontmatter, the invocation distinction, progressive disclosure, and how published collections organise their skills. Reference material about a format ORE Studio does not own.
#+type: knowledge
#+level: cross
#+filetags: :external:llm:claude_code:skills:reference:
#+created: 2026-08-26
#+updated: 2026-08-26

* Summary

A *skill* in agent tooling is a document that an assistant loads to
perform a kind of work. Anthropic defines the format for Claude Code:
a directory holding a =SKILL.md= file, whose frontmatter carries a name
and a description, and whose body holds the instructions the assistant
follows. Other agent tools read the same format.

This page records the received notion and the conventions that have
grown around it. ORE Studio does not own the format. For the narrower
definition this project works to, see [[id:87D41A08-0B37-41CE-8483-B59B36BA87FA][The skill in the compass
framework]].

* Detail

** The format

A skill is a directory. It contains a =SKILL.md= file and any supporting
files that file refers to. The frontmatter carries two required fields.
The =name= field gives the identifier a user types. The =description=
field states what the skill does and when to reach for it.

The body holds the instructions. Its length is not fixed by the format,
and published skills range from two lines to several hundred.

** Invocation

Published collections separate skills by who may invoke them. A
*user-invoked* skill runs only when a person types its name. A
*model-invoked* skill may also be reached by the assistant when the task
matches its description. Claude Code expresses the first with a
=disable-model-invocation= flag.

The distinction matters because the description does different work in
each case. For a model-invoked skill the description is the trigger, and
its wording decides how reliably the skill fires. For a user-invoked
skill the description is documentation.

** Progressive disclosure

A skill body sits in the assistant's context whenever the skill runs.
Long bodies therefore cost attention. The common answer is to move
material into sibling files and refer to them from the body, so the
assistant loads them only when it needs them.

The technique has a cost of its own. Material behind a reference is
reached only if the referring sentence is worded well enough to trigger
the read.

** In the literature

The construct has begun to receive formal treatment. Liu, Ming, Joty and
Zhao characterise the prevailing representation and find it wanting.
Skills, they write, "are injected into prompts, retrieved as advice, or
used indirectly to shape rewards during post-training", and are
therefore "largely /advisory/". The deficiency they name is precise:

#+begin_quote
A textual skill can express what the agent should do in principle, but
not precisely /when/ it should activate inside the policy loop, /how/ it
should alter the next decision.
#+end_quote

They state the gap as one "between reusable experience expressed in
language and reusable experience that can reliably and explicitly
control agent behavior", and survey prior systems as reusing "experience
as prompt text or task-specific routines".

Their own proposal replaces the text with an executable module carrying
two methods: =should_activate=, "which decides whether the skill should
fire", and =intervene=, "which returns the repair". Intervention takes
one of two forms, either modifying the next proposed action or injecting
corrective context into the agent's reasoning.

The paper is cited here for its characterisation of the received notion
rather than for its architecture, which addresses model training and
lies outside this project's concerns.

** How published collections organise skills

Three public collections show three different organising choices.

The *pstack* collection divides its skills into three kinds. Twenty-one
/principles/ each state one rule. Twenty-two /playbooks/ each give the
steps for a shape of work. The remaining skills are workflow tools. One
skill, a sticky mode, routes work to the others.

The *Matt Pocock* collection divides on invocation. User-invoked skills
are thin and orchestrate; model-invoked skills hold the reusable
discipline. A user-invoked skill may call a model-invoked one, and never
another user-invoked one.

The *Council of High Intelligence* ships one skill and eighteen
subagents. The skill is a coordinator. Each subagent supplies one
analytical lens.

None of the three registers a skill against the kind of artefact it acts
on. Each organises by what the skill /is/, rather than by what it acts
/upon/.

In the vocabulary of the paper cited above, all three consist of
/prompt-only/ skills. None carries an activation predicate that the
runtime can evaluate; each relies on the assistant reading a description
and judging that it applies. The paper reserves the term /program
function/ for a skill that carries such a predicate, and reports that
its own libraries mix the two kinds rather than using one exclusively.

One of the three anticipates the finding. The pstack collection includes
a principle named /encode lessons in structure/, whose rule is to
express a recurring correction "as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check,
or script instead of more text". That is the paper's thesis reached
independently by a practitioner, and stated as advice within a
prompt-only skill, which is the position it argues against.
